question: A constant flow of incidents is causing the Greek public health system to collapse under the pressure. Meanwhile, the country is being driven into poverty. In one recent incident, the child psychiatric unit at the University General Hospital of Heraklion (Crete’s largest hospital), the only unit of its kind on the island and in the whole South Aegean, closed despite cases of adolescent bullying.

How serious cases will be transferred to Athens is anybody’s guess. This same hospital is under strain due to staff shortages with 650 unfilled permanent posts and 5 200 patients on the waiting list for surgery. Meanwhile, the government is championing healthcare privatisation, establishing fee-paying afternoon surgeries in public hospitals.

The measure is a first in the country’s history and benefits only the welloff, exacerbating social inequality. In response to citizens’ objections to the new measure, Prime Minister Mitsotakis1 and the Minister of Health, Mr Georgiadis2, announced that afternoon surgeries would be free to begin with because they would be funded by the Recovery Fund.
The announcement makes the EU look like an accomplice in the dismantling of the health system. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Has temporary funding from the Recovery Fund been approved for the afternoon surgeries?
What steps does it plan to take to avoid giving the impression that it has a part to play in the destruction of public infrastructure and the widening of the gap between rich and poor?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.6.2024) According to Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU1, Member States are responsible for the organisation and delivery of health services and medical care, including the management thereof and the allocation of the resources assigned to them.

Without prejudice to these national responsibilities, the current grant component of the Greek Recovery and Resilience plan (RRP) includes reforms and investments with estimated costs equal to EUR 1 485 million to improve resilience, accessibility and sustainability of the healthcare system.

An additional EUR 367 million (EU allocation) has been allocated under the European Regional Development Fund to co-finance infrastructure and equipment at all levels of care in the Greek national health system in all 13 regions. Also, around EUR 250 million are allocated by the European Social Fund Plus towards investments to improve the accessibility and effectiveness of Greek healthcare services.

All these financial measures are expected to lead to improved health services in Greece and support the principle of equal access to health services, efficiency and social cohesion. Introducing new measures or modifications to the RRP requires a request for amendment of the RRP compliant with Article 21 of the Recovery and Resilience Facility Regulation2.
